 1             Pursuant to Civil L.R. 6-2, and this Court’s Standing Order for Civil Cases ¶ 7, Plaintiffs

 2   Yuchen “Justin” Sun (“Mr. Sun”), Blue Anthem Limited (“Blue Anthem”), and Black Anthem

 3   Limited (“Black Anthem”) (collectively, “Plaintiffs”), and Defendant World Liberty Financial

 4   LLC (f/k/a World Liberty Financial, Inc.) (“Defendant” or “World Liberty”), by and through their

 5   respective counsel of record, stipulate as follows:

 6             WHEREAS, on April 27, 2026, the Court set the initial Case Management Conference in

 7   this case for July 30, 2026. ECF No. 19.

 8             WHEREAS, on June 2, 2026, World Liberty filed its Motion to Compel Arbitration and its

 9   Motion to Dismiss. ECF Nos. 40-41.

10             WHEREAS, on June 5, 2026, this Court entered an order granting the parties’ joint

11   stipulation to extend the briefing deadlines for the Motion to Compel Arbitration, and sua sponte

12   ordered that briefing on the Motion to Dismiss was stayed pending further order. ECF No. 44.

13             WHEREAS, the hearing on World Liberty’s Motion to Compel Arbitration is currently

14   scheduled for August 20, 2026, three weeks after the initial Case Management Conference. ECF

15   No. 40.

16             WHEREAS, Civil L.R. 6-1(b) provides that “[a] Court order is required for any

17   enlargement or shortening of time that alters an event or deadline already fixed by Court order or

18   that involves papers required to be filed or lodged with the Court (other than an initial response to

19   the complaint). A request for a Court order enlarging or shortening time may be made by written

20   stipulation pursuant to Civil L.R. 6-2 or motion pursuant to Civil L.R. 6-3. Any stipulated request

21   or motion which affects a hearing or proceeding on the Court’s calendar must be filed no later than

22   14 days before the scheduled event.”

23             WHEREAS, this Court’s Standing Order for Civil Cases ¶ 7 provides that “[a]ny request

24   to reschedule a case management conference must be made in writing, by stipulation if possible,

25   not less than 10 calendar days before the conference date. Good cause must be shown. The

26   conference date will not be rescheduled unless the Court grants the request. Parties cannot change
27   the date by stipulation.”

 1             WHEREAS, good cause exists to reschedule the initial Case Management Conference

 2   pending resolution of Defendant’s Motion to Compel Arbitration. Proceeding with the initial Case

 3   Management Conference before the Motion to Compel Arbitration is even heard, let alone decided,

 4   would be premature and inefficient. If the request to compel arbitration is granted, certain claims,

 5   but not necessarily all claims, of Plaintiffs Blue Anthem Limited and Black Anthem Limited will

 6   be resolved in arbitration, and, if the accompanying request to stay is granted, any claims not sent

 7   to arbitration will be stayed, rendering the initial Case Management Conference and any case

 8   schedule set therein moot.

 9             WHEREAS, this Court has previously vacated initial case management conferences

10   pending resolution of a motion to compel arbitration. See Faridian v. DoNotPay, Inc., No. 3:23-

11   cv-01692-JD, Dkt. No. 41 (N.D. Cal. June 16, 2023) (vacating initial CMC and discovery hearing

12   “pending further order” while motion to compel arbitration was under submission). More broadly,

13   this Court has also vacated initial case management conferences sua sponte when a threshold

14   dispositive motion is pending. See Cherkin v. PowerSchool Holdings, Inc., No. 3:24-cv-02706-

15   JD, Dkt. No. 51 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 5, 2024) (vacating initial CMC and stating the Court would issue

16   a scheduling order after resolving pending motion to dismiss); see also Quamina v. JustAnswer

17   LLC, No. 3:22-cv-06051-JD, Dkt. No. 30 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 11, 2023) (continuing case management

18   conference in light of pending motion to compel arbitration);

19             WHEREAS, separate and apart from the above, good cause further exists because lead

20   counsel for Defendant has a pre-existing conflict on July 30, 2026, and the Court’s Standing Order

21   for Civil Cases ¶ 5 requires that “[f]or parties with counsel, each party must be represented at the

22   case management conference by lead counsel prepared to address all pertinent matters and with

23   authority to enter into stipulations and make admissions.”;

24             WHEREAS, in light of the above, Plaintiffs and Defendant have reached an agreement to

25   reschedule the Case Management Conference currently set for July 30, 2026 to a date 30 days after

26   the issuance of a decision on Defendant’s Motion to Compel Arbitration (ECF No. 40), or at the

 1          Plaintiffs Yuchen “Justin” Sun (“Mr. Sun”), Blue Anthem Limited, and Black Anthem

 2   Limited (collectively, “Plaintiffs”) respectfully submit this opposition in part to the Interim

 3   Administrative Motion to File Under Seal (ECF No. 43) (the “Motion to Seal”) filed by Defendant

 4   World Liberty Financial LLC (f/k/a World Liberty Financial, Inc.) (“World Liberty”).

 5          When Plaintiffs filed this action, they redacted limited portions of their Complaint that

 6   referred to an agreement containing a confidentiality provision. (ECF No. 1). That provision was

 7   the only reason Plaintiffs redacted any of their Complaint at all, and Plaintiffs carefully

 8   circumscribed their redactions to go no further than the provision required. (See ECF Nos. 1, 3, 3-

 9   2). Indeed, Plaintiffs took no position on whether the redacted material actually warranted sealing

10   and provisionally filed it under seal to give World Liberty an opportunity to establish the

11   requirements for sealing, as Plaintiffs explained in their Administrative Motion to Consider Whether

12   Defendant’s Material Should be Sealed Pursuant to Civil Local Rule 79-5(f). (See ECF No. 3).

17   dismiss and to compel arbitration (see ECF No. 43), including two agreements between the parties

18   that contain no confidentiality provisions and that Plaintiffs have never understood to be

19   confidential: the November 25, 2024 Token Purchase Agreement (“TPA”) by which Plaintiffs

20   acquired two billion of the digital tokens at the center of this case for $30 million (ECF No. 43-5),

21   and an Advisor Token Agreement (“ATA”) dated the same day, which memorialized World

23   advisor (ECF No. 43-6). (See ECF No. 1 ¶¶ 7-8). These agreements are foundational to the case.

24   Indeed, the Complaint mentions the TPA more than 50 times and quotes it liberally throughout.

 2   Liberty’s papers would be inconsistent with what was already publicly filed in the Complaint.

 3            World Liberty’s position contradicts the governing law. World Liberty fails to show either

 4   “compelling reasons” or “good cause” to seal the agreements. See Center for Auto Safety v. Chrysler

 5   Grp., LLC, 809 F.3d 1092, 1096-1102 (9th Cir. 2016) (courts require “compelling reasons” to seal

 6   motions that are “more than tangentially related to the merits of a case” and lesser “good cause”

 7   showing to seal motions “not related, or only tangentially related, to the merits of a case”).1

 8   Although World Liberty’s counsel asserts in conclusory terms that the company will suffer

 9   competitive harm if the agreements—now more than a year and a half old—are disclosed (see ECF

10   Nos. 43 at 4-5, 43-1 at 1-2), World Liberty offers no proof besides its own say-so. That is plainly

11   insufficient. Courts do not hesitate to deny sealing, even under the less-demanding “good cause”

12   standard, where—as here—a movant claims that “competitors could use the information to

13   ‘undercut [its] competitive standing in current and future contract negotiations’ but fails to show

17   2020), which World Liberty acknowledges it must clear at least as to its motion to dismiss.

19   World Liberty “has not shown why its preference for secrecy establishes a compelling reason to

20   override the judicial system’s ‘strong presumption’ in favor of public access to judicial records and

21   documents.” Avila v. Ford Motor Co., 821 F. Supp. 3d 1113, 1125 (N.D. Cal. 2026). This Court

22   should therefore deny World Liberty’s Motion to Seal to the extent it covers the TPA, the ATA, and

12           The Federal Arbitration Act embodies a “national policy favoring arbitration and a liberal

13 federal policy favoring arbitration agreements.” AT&T Mobility LLC v. Concepcion, 563 U.S. 333,

14 346 (2011) (citations omitted). In determining whether to compel arbitration under the FAA, a court

15 need only evaluate two “gateway” issues: (1) whether there is a valid agreement to arbitrate between

16 the parties; and (2) whether the agreement covers the dispute. Henry Schein, Inc. v. Archer & White

17 Sales, Inc., 586 U.S. 63, 67-68 (2019); Bielski v. Coinbase, Inc., 87 F.4th 1003, 1009 (9th Cir. 2023).

18 “If the response is affirmative on both counts, then the Act requires the court to enforce the

19 arbitration agreement in accordance with its terms.” Chiron Corp. v. Ortho Diag. Sys., Inc., 207

20 F.3d 1126, 1130 (9th Cir. 2000). The FAA “leaves no place for the exercise of discretion by a
21 district court, but instead mandates that district courts shall direct the parties to proceed to arbitration

22 on issues as to which an arbitration agreement has been signed.” Dean Witter Reynolds, Inc. v.

23 Byrd, 470 U.S. 213, 218 (1985) (emphasis in original). In such a case, the FAA “requires federal
24 district courts to stay judicial proceedings and compel arbitration of claims covered by a written and

25 enforceable arbitration agreement.” Nguyen v. Barnes & Noble Inc., 763 F.3d 1171, 1175 (9th Cir.

26 2014). For a dispute to be subject to a contractual agreement to arbitrate, the dispute “need only

27 ‘touch matters’ covered by the contract containing the arbitration clause.” Simula, Inc. v. Autoliv,

10 v. Terminix Consumer Servs., LLC, 817 F. Supp. 3d 1338, 1343-44 (N.D. Ga. 2025) (compelling

11 arbitration in part because “this litigation likely cannot be resolved without reference” to the

12 agreements with arbitration provisions, which “strengthen[s] the connection between [plaintiff’s]

13 claims and the parties’ agreement”).

15 confirms that they understood their claims were subject to AAA arbitration. This is reason enough

16 to compel arbitration. See Gestetner Holdings, PLC v. Nashua Corp., 784 F. Supp. 78, 82-83 n.4

 5 sole remaining Plaintiff once the Anthem Parties are compelled to arbitration.
 6          Under these circumstances, the Court can—and should—stay the remaining case pending
 7 completion of the arbitration. Such a stay is authorized by the FAA. 9 U.S.C. § 3 (if court finds a

 8 dispute arbitrable, the court “shall . . . stay the trial of the action until such arbitration has been
 9 had”). “In cases where the FAA is implicated, public policy and the orderly course of justice favor

10 staying a civil action that may implicate compelled arbitration.” Zamudio v. Aerotek, Inc, 2024 WL

11 863715, at *3 (E.D. Cal. Feb. 28, 2024). In determining whether to stay non-arbitrable claims

12 pending arbitration, “a court considers economy and efficiency, the similarity of the issues of law

13 and fact to those that will be considered during arbitration, and the potential for inconsistent findings

14 absent a stay.” Trinchitella v. Am. Realty Partners, LLC, 2016 WL 4041319, at *13 (E.D. Cal. July

15 27, 2016).

17 Allowing Sun to proceed in court while the Anthem Parties are arbitrating their claims would create

18 duplicative work across two venues for identical claims, causing waste of the Court’s, the

19 arbitrator’s, and the parties’ time and resources. While Sun’s claims should be dismissed, if they

20 are not, the issues for Sun’s claims and the Anthem Parties’ claims are not just similar—they are
21 identical. Sun brings exactly the same claims as the Anthem Parties, and litigating his claims will

                                        NATURE OF THIS ACTION

               1.     This case arises out of a campaign of defamatory statements published by

disclosed to Sun, including publicly available terms of sale and in a Token Unlock Agreement to

which Blue Anthem assented. Nevertheless, rather than work constructively with World Liberty

to address the misconduct, Sun embarked on a scorched-earth pressure campaign against World

Liberty to try to extract hundreds of millions of dollars from World Liberty, including having his

counsel threaten litigation designed to “light World Liberty on fire” and cause the $WLFI token

price to “go to shit.”

         4.     When World Liberty refused to capitulate to Sun’s threats, Sun launched his public

smear campaign. Beginning on April 12, 2026, Sun posted to his nearly four million X followers

that World Liberty deceived purchasers by “embedd[ing] a backdoor blacklisting function in the

smart contract used to deploy WLFI tokens,” which Sun called a “trap door” and part of a

“scandal[]” by “bad actors” at World Liberty. Sun also alleged that World Liberty took actions to

“extract fees from users” and that World Liberty “treat[s] the crypto community as a personal

ATM.” Sun further claimed that World Liberty’s pioneering governance process was “not

conducted through a fair or transparent process” and that outcomes of governance votes were

“predetermined.”

         5.     Sun followed up with three additional posts repeating and amplifying these false

claims, attacking a new governance proposal as an “absurd governance scam” and “coercion.”
